name: bench
description: USB hardware discovery for your AI tools: find maker boards (Arduino, ESP32, Pico), their serial ports and chips, plus skills for bring-up, serial debugging, crash decoding and safe flashing.
long_description:
Bench is a native macOS MCP server for developers who work with boards plugged into their Mac: Arduino, ESP32, Raspberry Pi Pico and other USB boards. It names the board, finds its serial port, reads and writes that port, detects the chip, decodes crash dumps, and flashes firmware with your approval. Device writes ask you first, every approval is logged, and Bench makes no network calls. Bench is free and open source, made by Seaynic Labs.

This bundle runs on Apple Silicon and Intel Macs with macOS 14 or later. The `debug` module (`decode_crash`) is off by default; set `BENCH_DEBUG_ENABLED=1` in the server's environment to switch it on.

tools.name: ping
tools.description: Check if Bench is running and IOKit is available

tools.name: list_usb_devices
tools.description: List all connected USB devices with type, vendor, product, and serial information

tools.name: get_device_info
tools.description: Get detailed information about a specific USB device by serial number, location ID, or name

tools.name: identify_device
tools.description: Identify a connected USB device — recognizes common maker boards (Arduino, Raspberry Pi Pico, ESP32, etc.) and provides context about the device

tools.name: eject_device
tools.description: Safely unmount and eject a removable USB storage device

tools.name: list_serial_ports
tools.description: Enumerate all serial ports on the system with their associated USB device info, type classification, and matched device details

tools.name: hub_topology
tools.description: Display the USB hub topology tree showing which devices are connected to which hubs and ports, with speeds and power draw

tools.name: tag_device
tools.description: Set, get, list, or remove persistent user-defined aliases (tags) for USB devices. Tags are stored locally and survive reconnections.

tools.name: port_reset
tools.description: Reset a USB port to recover a frozen or unresponsive device. Simulates an unplug/replug cycle via IOKit re-enumeration. Only works on external/removable devices.

tools.name: power_info
tools.description: Report USB power draw and capabilities for devices — bus power available, current draw, self-powered vs bus-powered, hub power budgets, and charging type detection

tools.name: monitor_events
tools.description: Monitor USB connect/disconnect events. Uses a polling approach — first call snapshots current state, subsequent calls report what changed since last check. Maintains a circular buffer of the last 50 events.

tools.name: snapshot_state
tools.description: Capture and compare USB device state snapshots. Save current state to a named snapshot, list snapshots, compare two snapshots or compare a snapshot to current state, or delete a snapshot.

tools.name: diagnose_device
tools.description: Query macOS system logs and IOKit for USB errors related to a specific device. Reports error count, error types, and recent log entries.

tools.name: device_descriptors
tools.description: Read full USB descriptor chain for a device — device descriptor, configuration descriptors, interface descriptors, and endpoint descriptors with class codes, transfer types, and max packet sizes

tools.name: flash_firmware
tools.description: Flash firmware to a USB device. Supports ESP32 (esptool), STM32 (dfu-util), Arduino AVR (avrdude), and RP2040 (UF2 copy). Shows the exact command before executing. Requires confirm=true — flashing is destructive.

tools.name: chip_detect
tools.description: Detect the exact chip type of a connected microcontroller via esptool. Resolves ambiguous USB identifications (e.g. ESP32-S2 vs S3 when sharing PID 0x1001). Returns chip type, revision, features, crystal frequency, and MAC address.

tools.name: hid_send
tools.description: Interact with USB HID (Human Interface Devices). Send output/feature reports, read input/feature reports, or list available report descriptors. Useful for controlling Stream Decks, macro pads, and custom HID devices.

tools.name: serial_open
tools.description: Open a serial connection to a port (e.g. /dev/cu.usbserial-2120). Configures baud rate, data bits, stop bits, and parity for raw communication.

tools.name: serial_read
tools.description: Read available data from an open serial connection. Returns whatever is in the receive buffer, waiting up to the timeout for data to arrive.

tools.name: serial_write
tools.description: Write data or a command to an open serial connection. Text is sent as UTF-8 with \r\n appended. Hex bytes can be sent as '0x01 0xFF' or '01FF'.

tools.name: serial_write_and_expect
tools.description: Write a line to an open serial connection, then read until a regex matches or the timeout passes. Returns the transcript and whether the pattern matched. Needs approval, like serial_write.

tools.name: decode_crash
tools.description: Decode an ESP32 Guru Meditation Error backtrace or an ARM HardFault register dump into source file and line, using addr2line and the matching .elf file. Read-only. Needs the toolchain's addr2line on PATH, or BENCH_ADDR2LINE set.

tools.name: serial_close
tools.description: Close an open serial connection and restore the port to its original state.

tools.name: serial_monitor
tools.description: Read from a serial port for a specified duration and return all output. Useful for capturing boot output, log streams, or device responses. Can auto-open the port if not already open.

tools.name: bench_modules
tools.description: List Bench modules: id, title, whether each is enabled in this server, its tools, and how to switch it on or off. Call this first to see what is available.

prompts.name: board-bring-up
prompts.description: Bring a new or unknown USB maker board (Arduino, ESP32, Raspberry Pi Pico, STM32) from plugged-in to talking over serial, using Bench. Use when the user connects a board for the first time, asks which board or chip they have, cannot find the board's port, or wants to confirm a board works before writing code.
prompts.text:
# Board bring-up

Goal: name the board and chip, find its serial port, read its boot output, and prove a write and a reply both work. Stop at each step that fails and fix it before the next one.

## 1. Confirm the board is visible

Call `list_usb_devices`. Look for the board by name, vendor or product. Record its serial number and location ID.

- Not listed: the cable carries power only, or the board is not enumerated. Ask the person to try a data cable and a different port. Call `monitor_events` once (the first call takes a snapshot), have the person unplug and replug the board, then call `monitor_events` again. A connect event in the second reply means the board enumerated.
- Listed as a generic name: go on to step 2. `identify_device` resolves it.

## 2. Name the board

Call `identify_device` with the serial number. Bench matches the vendor and product IDs against its database of known maker boards and returns the matched board with Bench's notes on it.

Some boards share one USB product ID. ESP32-S2 and ESP32-S3 do, for example. When the answer names more than one family, go to step 4 and call `chip_detect` to settle it.

## 3. Find the serial port

Call `list_serial_ports` with `device_type: usb`. Each entry gives a `/dev/cu.*` path and the USB device it matches. Use the `/dev/cu.*` form in every serial tool. A board can show two ports (for example a USB-serial bridge and a native USB port). Use the one whose matched device is the board.

If no port is listed for a board that appears in step 1, the board has no serial interface. Use `hub_topology` or `device_descriptors` to see its interfaces, and say so to the person.

## 4. Confirm the chip (ESP32 and similar)

Call `chip_detect` with the identifier. It runs esptool, which resets the chip into its bootloader. It needs approval, so the person sees the call first.

Read back the chip type, revision and MAC address. Record them in the reply. If esptool is missing, the error names the install command: install it and retry.

## 5. Read the boot output

1. `serial_open` with the port and the baud rate the firmware uses. Use `115200` when the person does not know. ESP32 boot ROM messages come out at 115200.
2. `serial_monitor` with `seconds: 5`. It reads without approval and returns what the board printed in those seconds.

Reading the output:

- Readable text: the baud rate is right. Note the firmware version or banner.
- Garbage characters: the baud rate is wrong. Close the port with `serial_close`, reopen at 9600 and then 74880, and monitor again.
- Repeating reset lines or a `Guru Meditation Error`: the firmware crashes on boot. Go to the serial-debugging skill.
- Nothing at all: the firmware may not print on this port, or it may wait for input. Monitor for 10 seconds, then check the sketch calls `Serial.begin`.

## 6. Prove a round trip

Pick a command the person's firmware answers. If none is known, use the firmware's `echo` or `ping` command if it has one, or ask the person for one.

Call `serial_write_and_expect` with the port, the command as `data`, a `pattern` for the expected reply (for example `^OK` or `pong`), and `timeout: 5`. It needs approval.

- Match: the board is working end to end. Report the matched text.
- No match within the timeout: read the transcript in the error. It shows what the board sent back. Adjust the pattern, not the timeout, when the reply is different text.

## 7. Clean up

Call `serial_close` on the port. An open session can block the next tool that needs the port, such as a flasher.

## Report

Give the person one short block: board name, chip and revision (if checked), port path, baud rate, the boot banner or first line, and the round-trip result. Name any step that did not pass, and the exact error code.

prompts.name: getting-started
prompts.description: Set up and check Bench, the USB hardware MCP server, and find out what it can see. Use when the user installs Bench, asks what Bench can do, sees a bench.<module>.<code> error, a module_disabled or write_not_approved error, or wants to turn a Bench module on or off.
prompts.text:
# Getting started with Bench

Bench lets you see USB boards (Arduino, ESP32, Raspberry Pi Pico and others), find their serial ports, read and write those ports, detect chips, and flash firmware. It runs on this Mac and makes no network calls.

Bench is split into modules. Each module can be switched on or off:

| Module | Tools | Default |
|---|---|---|
| core | `ping`, `bench_modules` | always on |
| usb | `list_usb_devices`, `get_device_info`, `identify_device`, `hub_topology`, `diagnose_device`, `device_descriptors`, `power_info`, `monitor_events`, `snapshot_state`, `tag_device`, `port_reset`, `eject_device` | on |
| serial | `list_serial_ports`, `serial_open`, `serial_read`, `serial_write`, `serial_write_and_expect`, `serial_monitor`, `serial_close` | on |
| firmware | `chip_detect`, `flash_firmware` | on |
| hid | `hid_send` | on |
| debug | `decode_crash` | off (new in 0.4.0) |

## 1. Check the server

Call `bench_modules`. It lists each module as `[on]` or `[off]`, every tool in it, the skills folder, and whether device writes are pre-approved.

Then call `ping`. It returns the server version and confirms IOKit answers.

If the person has a terminal, have them run `bench --doctor`. It prints one line per check and a `FIX` line for each problem, then exits 0 when everything is ready and 1 when something needs fixing. Pass each FIX line on as written.

## 2. Turn modules on or off

Set these in the environment of the MCP client, then restart the client:

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `BENCH_MODULES=usb,serial,firmware,hid` | Enables exactly this list. `core` is always on. |
| `BENCH_DEBUG_ENABLED=1` | Turns on one module, here `debug` (needed for `decode_crash`). |
| `BENCH_SERIAL_ENABLED=0` | Turns off one module, here `serial`. |

Tell the person which variable to add. Do not write these settings yourself.

## 3. Find the board

1. `list_usb_devices` lists every USB device with its name, vendor, product and serial number.
2. `identify_device` with the serial number (or location ID or name) names the matched board and Bench's notes on it.
3. `list_serial_ports` with `device_type: usb` shows the `/dev/cu.*` path for each board. Use that path in every serial tool.

## 4. Approvals

Tools that change a device ask the person to approve each call: `serial_write`, `serial_write_and_expect`, `flash_firmware`, `port_reset`, `eject_device`, `chip_detect` and `hid_send` (except its read actions). The prompt shows the full arguments.

- The approval comes from the person, through the client's prompt. A `confirm: true` argument that you pass does not count as approval.
- If the client cannot show prompts, the call fails with `bench.<module>.write_not_approved`. Tell the person to set `BENCH_APPROVE_DEVICE_WRITES=1` in the server's environment and restart. Do not set it yourself.
- Every approval asked, granted, declined or refused is written to `~/.local/state/bench/approvals.jsonl` (or the path in `BENCH_APPROVAL_LOG`). Arguments are redacted there. Point the person to that file when they ask what was approved.

## 5. Read errors

Every error reads `bench.<module>.<code>: <message> Fix: <hint>`. Pass the `Fix:` text to the person as written. The common codes:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `module_disabled` | The tool's module is off. Set the variable the hint names. |
| `missing_argument` | A required parameter is missing. Call again with it. |
| `port_not_open` | Run `serial_open` on the port first. |
| `write_not_approved` | The client cannot show approval prompts. See section 4. |
| `device_not_found` | Run `list_usb_devices` and use an identifier from it. |
| `toolchain_missing` | A flasher or addr2line is not on PATH. Install it, or set its full path in the environment. |

## 6. First session

Run these in order and report what each one shows:

1. `bench_modules`
2. `list_usb_devices` with `device_type: microcontroller`
3. `identify_device` on the board the person means
4. `list_serial_ports` with `device_type: usb`
5. `serial_monitor` on its port for 5 seconds, which reads boot output without any approval

prompts.name: safe-flashing
prompts.description: Flash firmware onto a USB maker board with Bench, safely, by checking the target, the file and the tool before the write. Use when the user asks to flash, upload, program or update a board's firmware, or when a flash fails with a tool error, a wrong-file error, or a timeout.
prompts.text:
# Safe flashing

Flashing overwrites the board's firmware. A wrong target or a wrong file can leave the board unbootable until someone reflashes it by hand. The steps below check the target, the file and the tool first, and each write needs the person's approval.

## 1. Identify the target

1. `list_usb_devices`, then `identify_device` with the board's serial number or location ID. Use that identifier for every later call. Do not use a name when two boards share one.
2. `chip_detect` (ESP32 and similar) to confirm the exact chip. It resets the chip into its bootloader, so the person approves it first.
3. Record the chip, the port path from `list_serial_ports`, and the board family.

If two or more boards of the same family are attached, stop. Ask the person which board is the target, and get its serial number.

## 2. Check the firmware file

Call nothing that writes yet. Check the file yourself:

| Target | Expected file | Tool Bench picks |
|---|---|---|
| ESP32, ESP32-S2, S3, C3 | `.bin` | esptool |
| STM32 in DFU mode | `.bin` | dfu-util |
| Arduino Uno, Nano, Mega (AVR) | `.hex` | avrdude |
| Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2040) | `.uf2` | uf2 (copies to the RPI-RP2 drive) |

Confirm the file exists, is not empty, and was built for this chip. Ask the person where it came from if the build output is unclear. A `.elf` cannot be flashed directly to most of these targets. Use the `.bin` or `.hex` the build produced next to it.

## 3. Close other sessions on the port

Call `serial_close` on the target's port if you opened it. A session open in Bench can block the flasher from using the port.

## 4. Read the approval, then flash

Call `flash_firmware` with:

- `identifier`: the serial number or location ID from step 1
- `firmware_path`: the absolute path to the file from step 2
- `tool`: only when auto-detection picked the wrong one. Use `esptool`, `dfu-util`, `avrdude` or `uf2`.
- `port`: only to override the detected port. It must be a `/dev/cu.*` path.
- `confirm`: `true`

The approval prompt shows these arguments. Read them against steps 1 and 2 before the person approves. If anything differs (another identifier, another file, a file from another project), do not approve it: tell the person what differs.

`confirm: true` must be set only for a call the person has approved in the prompt. A flash with `confirm` unset or false is refused, and that is correct.

If the client cannot show approval prompts, the call fails with `write_not_approved`. Tell the person to set `BENCH_APPROVE_DEVICE_WRITES=1` themselves and restart the client. Do not set it.

## 5. Verify the result

1. Read the tool's result. It names the tool used, the command it ran, and the exit status.
2. `serial_open` on the port at 115200 and `serial_monitor` with `seconds: 10`. A good flash shows the new firmware's boot banner.
3. A boot loop or a `Guru Meditation Error` after a successful flash points to a bad image, or a bootloader that does not match. Go to the serial-debugging skill, and do not flash again until the cause is known.
4. `serial_close` when done.

## Errors

| Code or message | What to do |
|---|---|
| "is not installed" | The flasher is missing. Install the tool the message names, put it on PATH, and retry. |
| "confirm must be true" | The call was made without `confirm`. Repeat it with `confirm: true` only after the approval. |
| "Could not auto-detect flashing tool" | Pass `tool` explicitly, using the table in step 2. |
| "Invalid port" | Use the `/dev/cu.*` path from `list_serial_ports`. |
| A timeout while writing | Put the board in its bootloader mode (hold BOOT, press RESET on most ESP32 boards), then retry. |
| Repeated failures | Stop after two. Report the tool's output and ask the person how to proceed. |

## Never

- Flash a board the person has not named by serial number or location.
- Flash a file that is not the one the person chose.
- Set `BENCH_APPROVE_DEVICE_WRITES` or any other environment variable.
- Retry a declined flash. A decline is the person's answer for that call.

prompts.name: serial-debugging
prompts.description: Debug a USB serial session with Bench when the device output is garbled, silent, looping, or does not reply to commands, or when the device crashed and printed a Guru Meditation Error or HardFault. Use when the user says their board prints nothing, prints junk, reboots in a loop, ignores commands, or shows a crash dump.
prompts.text:
# Serial debugging

Work from the cheapest check to the most expensive. Each step narrows the cause, and the approval-gated tools come last.

## 1. Read before writing

Use only the read tools first. They run without approval.

1. `serial_open` on the port with the baud rate the firmware sets (in its `Serial.begin` call or its config). Leave out `baud_rate` for 115200.
2. `serial_monitor` with `seconds: 10`.
3. Read the output and match it to a row below.

| Output | Likely cause | Next step |
|---|---|---|
| Readable text | Working link | Go to step 2 |
| Random bytes, `�` characters | Wrong baud rate | Reopen at 9600, 19200, 57600, 74880, 115200 and monitor each for 3 seconds. The right one reads cleanly. |
| Nothing for 10 seconds | Board silent, port wrong, or board waiting | Check the port with `list_serial_ports`. Try `serial_read` with `timeout: 3`. Send a newline with `serial_write` if the board waits for input. |
| The same boot lines repeat | Reset loop | Look for a crash line (step 4). |
| `Guru Meditation Error`, `Backtrace:` | ESP32 crash | Step 4 |
| `HardFault`, `CFSR`, `PC =` | ARM Cortex-M crash | Step 4 |

## 2. Confirm the reply path

Use `serial_write_and_expect` to send one command and wait for its reply. It needs approval, and the person sees the full command first.

- Set `pattern` to the exact text the firmware prints, as a regular expression. `^OK` matches a line that starts with OK. `temp=[0-9.]+` matches a reading.
- Set `timeout` to the longest the firmware takes to answer. 5 seconds covers most sketches.
- On no match, the error returns the last 8 KB of output. Compare it to the pattern before changing anything else.

A device that echoes the command but never replies usually has a line-ending mismatch. Send with a trailing newline in `data` (Bench adds CR LF when there is none) and try again.

## 3. Check the port is free

- `port_not_open`: `serial_open` was not called, or `serial_close` ran. Open the port again.
- `Read error` or `Write error`: the board was unplugged or reset. Run `list_serial_ports` again, since the path can change when the board re-enumerates.
- A second session on the same port: close one. Bench holds the port until `serial_close`.

## 4. Decode a crash

Crash dumps show code addresses that point into the firmware. `decode_crash` maps them to source lines.

Requirements:

- The `debug` module is on. Set `BENCH_DEBUG_ENABLED=1` in the client's environment and restart it. Tell the person to do this; do not set it yourself.
- An addr2line for the chip is on PATH: `xtensa-esp32-elf-addr2line` or `riscv32-esp-elf-addr2line` for ESP32 parts, `arm-none-eabi-addr2line` for ARM. Or set `BENCH_ADDR2LINE` to its full path.
- The `.elf` file from the same build that is crashing. A `.bin` or `.hex` will not work.

Call `decode_crash` with:

- `output`: the crash block, from the `Guru Meditation` or `HardFault` line through the `Backtrace:` or register lines.
- `elf`: the absolute path to the `.elf`, for example `/Users/you/project/build/firmware.elf`.

Read the frames top to bottom. Frame `#0` is the instruction that faulted. The rest are the calls that led there. A frame marked `??` is not in the `.elf`, which usually means the `.elf` is from a different build.

Then fix the code at frame `#0` or the first frame that is in the person's own source. Use the `systematic-debugging` skill to confirm the cause before changing code.

## 5. Common crash causes

- `LoadProhibited` or `StoreProhibited` on an address near 0 or in the 0x3ffb range: a null pointer, or a buffer written past its end.
- `IllegalInstruction` after a flash update: the firmware and bootloader do not match. Reflash the whole image.
- `InstrFetchProhibited` on an address in RAM: a function pointer or stack overflow jumped into data.
- `Stack overflow` or `Stack canary watchpoint`: a task stack is too small. Increase it or move large buffers off the stack.
- ARM `HardFault` with `IACCVIOL` or `IBUSERR`: a jump to a bad address, often a corrupted function pointer.
- ARM `HardFault` with `PRECISERR` or `BFARVALID`: the address in `BFAR` is the bad access.

## 6. When to stop and ask

Stop and ask the person before any of these:

- Re-flashing the board (see the safe-flashing skill).
- Changing any setting in the client's environment.
- Sending a command to a device the person has not named.

## Report

Give the person the port and baud rate, the first crash line or the matched reply, the decoded top frame with its file and line, and the next check you suggest.

prompts.name: systematic-debugging
prompts.description: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes
prompts.text:
# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: $([ -n "${IDENTITY:-}" ] && echo SET || echo UNSET)"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   printenv IDENTITY >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "IDENTITY in environment" || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?
   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.
